hints: Notice this reaction has hydrocarbons on both sides, so think about which Hess cycle lets you go via complete combustion to CO2 and H2O.
Write the Hess expression as sum of combustion enthalpies of reactants minus sum for products, remembering O2, CO2 and H2O(l) cannot burn further.
Apply the mole numbers from the equation, 2 moles of ethane reacting to make 2 moles of methane, to link the two combustible species.
walkthrough:
**Recall the combustion Hess rule**

Think of burning everything completely. Hess's Law gives a shortcut for any reaction.

$$\Delta H_r^\ominus = \sum \Delta H_c^\ominus(\text{reactants}) - \sum \Delta H_c^\ominus(\text{products})$$

**Sort out who can burn**

Only $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6$ and $\text{CH}_4$ are fuels. $\text{O}_2$ is already an element needed for burning, and $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$ are already the final combustion products.

So their $\Delta H_c^\ominus$ values are zero and drop out of the sum.

**Put in the stoichiometry**

From the equation we have 2 moles of reactant ethane and 2 moles of product methane.

$$\Delta H_r^\ominus = 2\Delta H_c^\ominus(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6) - 2\Delta H_c^\ominus(\text{CH}_4)$$

**Check the other routes**

A formation route would need $2 \times$ every product minus $2 \times$ reactant, with correct coefficients. A bond energy route would need bonds broken minus bonds made counted carefully for all molecules. Only the combustion expression matches correctly.

options.A: Incorrect. $\Delta H_c^\ominus(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6)$ alone is the enthalpy for $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6 + 3.5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$, not our reaction which also makes $\text{CH}_4$. You must subtract the combustion enthalpy of the methane product as well.
options.B: Correct. By Hess's Law, $\Delta H_r^\ominus = \sum \Delta H_c^\ominus(reactants) - \sum \Delta H_c^\ominus(products)$. This gives $2\Delta H_c^\ominus(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6) + 3\Delta H_c^\ominus(\text{O}_2) - [2\Delta H_c^\ominus(\text{CH}_4) + 2\Delta H_c^\ominus(\text{CO}_2) + 2\Delta H_c^\ominus(\text{H}_2\text{O})]$. Since $\Delta H_c^\ominus$ of $\text{O}_2$, $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$ is zero, this simplifies to $2\Delta H_c^\ominus(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6) - 2\Delta H_c^\ominus(\text{CH}_4)$.
options.C: Incorrect. Bond energy method is $\Delta H_r = \sum E(bonds broken) - \sum E(bonds made)$. This option miscounts bonds badly. For example, breaking 2 $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6$ alone breaks 2 C-C and 12 C-H bonds, and $\text{O}_2$, $\text{CH}_4$, $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ bonds are also mishandled, and C=O in $\text{CO}_2$ needs $4E(C=O)$ per $\text{CO}_2$ molecule.
options.D: Incorrect. The formation rule is right in principle, $\Delta H_r^\ominus = \sum \Delta H_f^\ominus(products) - \sum \Delta H_f^\ominus(reactants)$, but the coefficients are missing. It should be $2\Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{CH}_4) + 2\Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{CO}_2) + 2\Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{H}_2\text{O}) - 2\Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6)$. Forgetting to multiply by 2 is a classic trap.
